tagline: A former wagon route links Lake Superior, forest and five waterfalls
intro: Black River Scenic Byway follows County Road 513 through pine, hemlock and hardwood forest between Airport Road and Black River Harbor. The Forest Service describes an 11-mile drive and credits its scenery and recreation opportunities for the byway’s 1992 dedication. The road runs west of the Black River, back from its banks, with trails leading to five waterfalls.

A wagon road recorded in William A. Burt’s 1848 surveys connected the harbor site with Chippewa Hill, now the location of Copper Peak. Michigan built a waterfront-to-Bessemer wagon road in 1904; a county road followed by 1927. The county had purchased waterfront land for a park in 1924. Fishing-village residents were forced to move and settled at Black River Village. Local officials proposed National Forest Scenic Byway status in 1991, and the Forest Service conferred it in June 1992.

Traveling south from Lake Superior, begin at Black River Harbor and work inland past access to Rainbow, Sandstone, Gorge, Potawatomi and Great Conglomerate Falls. Copper Peak comes next, where the road curves away from the river. Continue through the forest to Airport Road, the designated drive’s southern end; County Road 513 carries on toward US 2 near Bessemer.

moments.title: Black River Harbor
moments.text: A wooden suspension bridge carries the North Country Trail across the Black River at the harbor. The crossing also leads to a trail reaching Lake Superior’s sand-and-stone shoreline. The harbor occupies the site of a 1920s fishing village. In 1967, Gogebic County exchanged its riverside park land, including the harbor, with the Forest Service. A historic pavilion built by the Civilian Conservation Corps overlooks the harbor, lake and picnic area. After crossing the river, the North Country Trail continues east toward Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park. Inside the pavilion are tables and a fireplace.
moments.notice: The wooden suspension bridge leads toward a shoreline of sand and stone.

moments.title: Great Conglomerate Falls
moments.text: A large conglomerate outcrop divides Great Conglomerate Falls in the middle of the Black River. The waterfall drops 30 feet; when summer water is lower, it separates into two drops. Its name comes from that outcrop. The Forest Service attributes the river’s color to tannin from hemlock trees. This is the southernmost of the five waterfall stops on the byway, before Copper Peak when traveling inland. The Forest Service describes short trails from paved parking lots to the waterfalls, with steps on most paths. The Forest Service reports major repairs to waterfall platforms and trails.
moments.notice: In lower summer water, the falls split into two drops beside the conglomerate outcrop.

moments.title: Copper Peak
moments.text: Copper Peak’s ski-slide and tower stand above a hill where mining failed to produce copper. The Chippewa Copper Mining Company began work in 1845, driving a tunnel into the rock, but produced no copper and closed. The 1845 tunnel and excavation pits remain visible on the hill. The ski tower rests on concrete footings set in solid rock; its construction did not disturb the earlier tunnel and excavation pits. Ski flying competitions began in 1970, with ten FIS-sanctioned competitions held through 1994. Landing-hill reconstruction was underway by May 2025, with completion scheduled for December 2026.

practical: Black River Harbor: Winter access to the day-use area and waterfall trailheads can be limited by snow plowing; services are reduced. (checked 2026-10-11)
